docs.title: From the Web-UI
docs.text: The experiment must be started; click on the experiment name to enter the Running Experiment component. Within that component, click on the checkbox adjacent to the VM Name column to select all the VMs. Alternatively, the checkbox adjacent to a specific VM name can be used to select the VM. Once one or more VMs are selected, a toolbar will appear to the left of the search text box. The buttons on the toolbar are essentially the same as described in VMs.

docs.title: From the Command Line Binary
docs.text:
Several phenix vm commands support selecting target VMs by label with -l / --label, or all VMs using all. When using labels, a VM name argument is not required.

Supported commands:

  • phenix vm info
  • phenix vm pause
  • phenix vm resume
  • phenix vm restart
  • phenix vm reset-disk
  • phenix vm redeploy
  • phenix vm shutdown
  • phenix vm kill

Behavior:

  • Multiple labels are supported and use OR semantics (a VM is selected if any label matches).
  • Labels support glob patterns (for example, ot-* or *-server).
  • The special label all selects every VM in the experiment.
  • Labels can be provided by repeating -l and/or as a comma-separated value.

Examples:

# Show VM info for all VMs with a label matching "ot-*"
phenix vm info <experiment name> --label ot-*

# Restart VMs that match either label
phenix vm restart <experiment name> -l control -l historian

# Pause VMs using comma-separated labels
phenix vm pause <experiment name> -l control,historian

# Shutdown all VMs in the experiment
phenix vm shutdown <experiment name> --label all

docs.title: Searching for VMs
docs.text: The search text box can be used to filter the list of VMs to only apply actions to the filtered list.

docs.title: From the Web-UI
docs.text:
The experiment must be started; click on the experiment name to enter the Running Experiment component. Within that component, use the search textbox to find VMs by:

  • state - The keywords running,shutdown,paused,capturing can be used to find VMs in a specific state. Also, the not keyword can be used to negate search term(s) (i.e. not running)

  • ipv4 address - VMs in a specific subnet can be found by entering the subnet (i.e 192.168.2.0/30)

  • other fields (i.e. name, taps, tags) - All other fields will be searched for a keyword contained within the field

  • combine search terms - Search terms can be combined by using or and keywords. Parenthesis can also be used to group search terms.

  • escape keywords - To find keywords that appear in a VM name use double quotes. For example, to find a VM named free_running, type "running".

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Multiple search terms

docs.title: From the Command Line Binary
docs.text:
While the interactive search bar is specific to the Web-UI, you can view and list all VMs in an experiment (or filter for specific VMs by name or label) using the phenix vm info command:

# List details for all VMs in an experiment
phenix vm info <experiment name>

# Display details for a specific VM in an experiment
phenix vm info <experiment name> <vm name>

# Filter VMs by label
phenix vm info <experiment name> --label <label>

docs.title: From the Web-UI
docs.text:
When a valid ipv4 subnet is entered, the play button adjacent to the IPv4 label will be enabled. To start capturing, press the play button.

Once there are valid captures, the stop button adjacent to the play button will be enabled. To stop all the captures, press the stop button.

To stop all packet captures for all subnets, the term capturing can be entered in the search bar to find all the VMs with active packet captures.

docs.title: From the Command Line Binary
docs.text:
To start packet captures on running VMs for a specific subnet, use the following command.

phenix vm capture start-subnet <experiment name> <subnet>

To stop all packet captures for a specific subnet, use the following command.

phenix vm capture stop-subnet <experiment name> <subnet>

To stop all packet captures for an experiment, use the following command.

phenix vm capture stop-all <experiment name>

docs.title: Stopped Experiment Component
docs.text:
Similar to the Running Experiment component, multiple VMs can be selected for the Stopped Experiment component. In addition, VMs in the Stopped Experiment component can be searched by:

  • state - The keyword dnb can be used to find all VMs with the do not boot flag set to true. Also, the not keyword can be used to negate search term(s) (i.e. not dnb)

  • ipv4 address - VMs in a specific subnet can be found by entering the subnet (i.e 192.168.2.0/30)

  • other fields (i.e. VM, host, disk)

  • combine search terms - Search terms can be combined by using or and keywords. Parenthesis can also be used to group search terms.

  • escape keywords - To find keywords that appear in a VM name use double quotes. For example, to find a VM named dnb_me, type "dnb".

docs.title: From the Web-UI
docs.text:
The experiment must be started; click on the experiment name to enter the Running Experiment component. Within that component, click on the VM name and you will be presented with a VM information modal.

Available commands

  • restore a snapshot by clicking the play button next to the desired snapshot name.

Buttons from left to right:

  • pause a running VM
  • Create a memory snapshot of a running VM
  • Create a backing image of a running VM
  • Create a snapshot of a running VM
  • record screenshot of a running VM
  • modify state opens another toolbar of buttons

docs.title: Modify State Toolbar
docs.text:
Buttons from left to right:

  • redeploy a running VM
  • reset disk state of a running VM
  • restart a running VM
  • shutdown a running VM
  • kill a running VM
  • close modify state toolbar

docs.title: From the Command Line Binary
docs.text:
There are two options for displaying the information for VMs in an experiment. First run the following command to see information for all VMs in a given experiment.

phenix vm info <experiment name>

Or, run the following to see the information for a specific VM in an experiment.

phenix vm info <experiment name> [vm name] [--label <label>]

docs.title: From the Command Line Binary

To create an ELF memory dump, run the following command.

phenix vm memory-snapshot <experiment name> <vm name> <snapshot file path>

docs.text: While ELF memory dumps can be created via phenix vm memory-snapshot, there is currently no CLI subcommand to take standard VM disk snapshots. VM disk snapshots are managed through the Web-UI and the REST API (POST /api/vms/snapshots).

docs.title: Mount a VM
docs.text:
The VM Mount feature lets you transfer files to and from a running VM directly through the phēnix Web-UI. It is an optional feature that must be enabled when starting the phēnix UI with the vm-mount feature flag (see Enabling VM Mount below).

Note

Mounting a VM requires the minimega command-and-control agent (miniccc) to be installed and actively running in the VM. If cc is not active for a VM, the mount button is disabled.

docs.title: Enabling VM Mount
docs.text:
VM Mount is disabled by default. Enable it by passing the vm-mount feature to the --features flag when starting the UI:

phenix ui --features vm-mount

The feature can also be enabled via the ui.features configuration key or the PHENIX_UI_FEATURES environment variable. See Settings & Configuration for details.

docs.title: From the Web-UI
docs.text:
The experiment must be started. Click on the name of a running VM to access the VM information modal, then click the mount vm button (the hard-drive icon).

The mount browser modal presents two panes:

  • Local file system — browse to a file on your local machine and upload it into the VM, or download a file from the VM to your local machine.
  • Experiment files — copy files that already exist on the phēnix server into the VM. This option is only available when the experiment file server is enabled (see below).

docs.title: Uploading Experiment Files from the phēnix Server
docs.text:
phēnix can optionally run a lightweight file server on a port separate from the main UI. This was added to support environments where the phēnix UI is only reachable on a private network but files (for example, application installers or configuration files) need to be uploaded to an experiment from a public network.

When the file server is enabled, the VM Mount modal gains the Experiment files option described above, allowing files that have been uploaded to an experiment to be copied directly into a VM without going through the user's local machine.

Enable the file server by passing the --file-server-endpoint flag when starting the UI:

# Bind to 127.0.0.1 on port 8080 (port-only value binds to localhost)
phenix ui --features vm-mount --file-server-endpoint 8080

# Bind to a specific interface and port
phenix ui --features vm-mount --file-server-endpoint 0.0.0.0:8080

The file server presents a simple interface for selecting an experiment and uploading a file to it. When authentication/authorization is enabled for the main phēnix UI, it is automatically enforced on the file server as well, so users must already have valid phēnix credentials to upload files. File upload permissions are included in the default Experiment Admin and Experiment User roles.

See Settings & Configuration for the ui.file-server-endpoint configuration key.

docs.title: From the Command Line Binary
docs.text:
Use phenix vm mount to mount a running VM's filesystem to a directory on the phēnix headnode. Unlike the Web-UI mount browser above, this does not require the vm-mount UI feature flag to be enabled, and the mounted filesystem is accessed directly on the headnode's filesystem rather than through the browser.

phenix vm mount <experiment name> <vm name> [host path]

If host path is omitted, the VM is mounted to a default path of <mount-dir>/<experiment name>/<vm name>, where <mount-dir> defaults to <base-dir.phenix>/mounts (see mount-dir). The command prints the resolved host path once the mount succeeds.

phenix vm mount my-exp my-vm
# VM my-vm in experiment my-exp mounted at: /phenix/mounts/my-exp/my-vm

phenix vm mount my-exp my-vm /tmp/my-vm-files
# VM my-vm in experiment my-exp mounted at: /tmp/my-vm-files

To unmount the VM's filesystem, run:

phenix vm unmount <experiment name> <vm name>

Note

Mounting a VM requires the minimega command-and-control agent (miniccc) to be installed and actively running in the VM; the command will fail if the agent is not reachable.

Mounts are automatically unmounted, and their mount directories removed, when the owning experiment is stopped or deleted, so mounts do not outlive their experiment.

docs.title: From the Web-UI
docs.text:
Click on the name of the network tap on a running VM in a started experiment to start a packet capture. The name of the network tap will turn green once a packet capture has started. It is possible to start captures on multiple network taps.

To stop a capture, click the name of a green network tap. If the VM has more than one capture running, phēnix asks whether to stop only that interface's capture or all packet captures for the VM.

docs.title: From the Command Line Binary
docs.text:
To start a packet capture, run the following command, specifying the target network interface by its name (as declared in the experiment topology, e.g. IF0) or its zero-based index.

phenix vm capture start <experiment name> <vm name> <iface name/index> </path/to/out file>

To stop all packet captures on a running VM, use the following command.

phenix vm capture stop <experiment name> <vm name>

To stop the packet capture running on a single interface, without affecting any other captures running on the same VM, provide the interface name or index.

phenix vm capture stop <experiment name> <vm name> <iface name/index>

Note

Stopping the capture on a single interface, from the Web-UI or the command line, requires minimega 3.3.0 or later.

docs.title: From the Web-UI
docs.text:
Click on the name of a running VM in a started experiment to access the VM information modal. Click the modify state button on the far right to open the modify state toolbar. Click the kill button as shown in the screenshot below.

Note: if you stop and then start the experiment again, that VM will run again per the experiment configuration.

phenix vm kill <experiment name> [vm name] [--label <label>]

docs.title: From the Web-UI

To revert back to previous setting, simply repeat selecting the network interface you wish to change, and select the previous network setting.

docs.title: From the Command Line Binary
docs.text:
To connect a VM network interface to a different network, run the following command.

phenix vm net connect <experiment name> <vm name> <iface index> <vlan id>

To disconnect a VM network interface, run the following command.

phenix vm net disconnect <experiment name> <vm name> <iface index>

docs.title: From the Web-UI
docs.text:
There are two ways to modify VM settings:

  1. Click on a stopped experiment to access the Stopped Component. You are able to edit the following:
    • Host name
    • CPUs
    • Memory
    • Disk
    • Do not boot flag
  2. From a running experiment, click on the VM name and then the redeploy button (yellow power button, second from the right on the modal footer). You are able to edit the following:
    • CPU
    • Memory
    • Disk
    • Replication of original injections

docs.title: From the Command Line Binary
docs.text:
To modify VM settings, run the following command, specifying one or more of the configuration flags described below.

phenix vm set <experiment name> [<vm name>] [flags]

Only the flags that are explicitly provided will be applied; any setting whose flag is omitted is left unchanged. The following flags are supported:

Flag Description -c, --cpu Number of VM CPUs (1-8 is valid). -m, --mem Amount of memory in megabytes (512, 1024, 2048, 3072, 4096, 8192, 12288, 16384 are valid). -d, --disk VM backing disk image. -p, --partition Partition of disk to inject files into. --do-not-boot Set the do-not-boot flag for the VM. --snapshot Set the snapshot (non-persistent) flag for the VM. -L, --label-changes key=value VM label to set, in key=value form. May be repeated to set multiple labels. --append-label Append the provided labels to the VM's existing labels instead of replacing them. -l, --label Apply the change to every VM whose label matches the provided label (supports glob patterns). Use all to select every VM in the experiment. May be repeated.

For example, to set the CPU count to 4 and memory to 2048 MB for a VM named my-vm in an experiment named my-exp:

phenix vm set my-exp my-vm --cpu 4 --mem 2048

To set the role=server labels on VMs whose existing labels matches tier=web* in the same experiment, without clearing the existing labels:

phenix vm set my-exp --label "tier=web*" -L role=server --append-labels

To set two labels on the VM my-vm and replace the existing labels on the VM:

phenix vm set my-exp my-vm -L val1=true -L val2=roger

Note

Only label updates and interface VLAN connections can be modified while an experiment is running. To change CPU, memory, disk, partition, do-not-boot, or snapshot settings, the experiment must be stopped. Use phenix vm net to modify interface VLAN connections on a running experiment.

docs.title: Applying Actions to Multiple VMs
docs.text:
Note

See VM Multi Action for documentation on applying actions to multiple VMs at once.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
A topology directory holds everything phēnix needs to run an experiment: its configs, the files to inject into its VMs, and a workflow config (phenix.yml) that says whether to create, update, start or restart the experiment. phenix workflow apply deploys such a directory in one command, and CI jobs and scripts can call the same REST API endpoints.

Note

phenix workflow apply runs on the phēnix host, or in the phēnix container, and talks to the running phenix ui server through its unix socket. Use a server from the same phēnix release as the CLI.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Create a topology directory with a topology config, a file to inject and a workflow config:

mkdir -p /phenix/topologies/helloworld/phenix-configs /phenix/topologies/helloworld/phenix-injects
cd /phenix/topologies/helloworld

echo "hello from phenix workflow apply" > phenix-injects/motd

cat > phenix-configs/topology.yml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Topology
metadata:
  name: ${BRANCH_NAME}
spec:
  nodes:
  - type: VirtualMachine
    general:
      hostname: host-01
    hardware:
      os_type: linux
      drives:
      - image: ubuntu.qc2
    network:
      interfaces:
      - name: IF0
        vlan: EXP
        address: 10.0.0.1
        mask: 24
        proto: static
        type: ethernet
    injections:
    - src: /phenix/injects/${BRANCH_NAME}/motd
      dst: /etc/motd
EOF

cat > phenix.yml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v0
kind: Workflow
metadata: {}
spec:
  auto:
    create: ${BRANCH_NAME}
  topology: ${BRANCH_NAME}
EOF

Check what phēnix would do, then deploy:

phenix workflow apply helloworld -n
phenix workflow apply helloworld
phenix experiment list

The dry run logs the plan (action=createAndStart, experiment=helloworld) and changes nothing. The second command copies phenix-injects/ to /phenix/injects/helloworld, creates the helloworld topology, and creates and starts the helloworld experiment. After you change the topology, run it again with -f to allow restarting the running experiment:

phenix workflow apply helloworld -f

docs.title: Topology Directory
docs.text:
helloworld/
├── phenix.yml          # workflow config
├── phenix-configs/     # topology, scenario and other configs
│   ├── topology.yml
│   └── scenario.yml
└── phenix-injects/     # files to inject into VMs
    └── motd

Every part is optional, and a missing part is skipped: a directory with only phenix-configs/ just creates or updates its configs. A directory with none of them is an error.

  • phenix.yml - the workflow config. A file with another name needs -c.
  • phenix-configs/ - one config per .json, .yaml or .yml file, in subdirectories too. Other files and hidden files are skipped. Each file holds one YAML or JSON document, and its kind must be written out, not given as a ${VAR} placeholder. Each config is created, or updated if it already exists.
  • phenix-injects/ - copied to <base-dir.injects>/<name> on the phēnix host, by default /phenix/injects/<name>, replacing any previous copy. By default, symlinks inside phenix-injects/ are copied as symlinks; --follow-inject-symlinks follows them and copies targets as regular files or directories.

docs.title: Branch Name
docs.text:
<name> is the workflow branch name: the directory's name, unless -b sets another. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, ., _ and -.

${BRANCH_NAME} in a config or in the workflow config expands to the branch name. The server keeps every other ${VAR} placeholder as written (see Environment Variables). Because only ${BRANCH_NAME} expands, configs reference injected files as /phenix/injects/${BRANCH_NAME}/<file>. Thus you can deploy one directory under several names side by side. A config's kind and metadata.name can use no placeholder but ${BRANCH_NAME}. An experiment that a workflow creates is mapped to its branch name.

Configs that hard-code the injects path need -b set to the name they use: a topology that references /phenix/injects/lab-a/<file> is deployed with phenix workflow apply ./site -b lab-a.

The names phenix.yml, phenix-configs and phenix-injects are reserved, in any letter case. A branch name can't be one of them, and they can't appear at the top level of phenix-injects/ or directly inside one of its top-level directories.

docs.title: The phenix workflow apply Command
docs.text:
phenix workflow apply <DIR|NAME> [flags]

DIR is the path of a topology directory; use . for the current directory. A NAME that isn't an existing path is looked up under base-dir.topologies, by default /phenix/topologies/NAME, so the command works from any directory.

Flag Default Description -b, --branch-name the directory's name The workflow branch name. -c, --config phenix.yml Workflow config file, relative to the directory unless absolute. -n, --dry-run false Validate everything, log the server's plan, and change nothing. -f, --force false Allow restarting a running experiment. --follow-inject-symlinks false Follow symlinks in phenix-injects/ and copy targets as regular files or directories.

The global flags --unix-socket, --base-dir.injects, --base-dir.topologies and --log.level also apply; see Global Flags.

The command never prompts. It reports through the phēnix logger and runs five steps, named in the step field of its log lines. Nothing changes before injects:

  1. preflight - checks that the server answers and that every file can be read and parsed.
  2. plan - the server dry-runs every config and the workflow config, and the plan is logged. -n stops here. Without -f, so does a plan that would restart a running experiment.
  3. injects - copies phenix-injects/ into place.
  4. configs - creates or updates each config, topologies first.
  5. apply - applies the workflow config: the server creates, updates, starts or restarts the experiment (see Actions).

The exit status is 0 when the run completed or a dry run passed, and non-zero otherwise.

The apply records where it came from in the experiment's phenix.workflow/tags annotation: method=workflow, the directory (dir), the branch name (branch), the time (workflow_date) and, when the directory is in a git work tree, the short commit, with a -dirty suffix for uncommitted changes.

Warning

Run the command from outside a topology directory you didn't write. phēnix reads its settings files (config.* and users.*) from the current directory first, so such a file in the directory could change the settings of the run.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
phenix workflow apply --help has the full list.

Command What it does phenix workflow apply /phenix/topologies/helloworld Deploy by path. The branch name is helloworld. phenix workflow apply helloworld Look up helloworld under base-dir.topologies. phenix workflow apply . Deploy the current directory. phenix workflow apply helloworld -n Validate everything and log the plan. phenix workflow apply helloworld -f Allow restarting the running experiment. phenix workflow apply helloworld -b helloworld-2 Deploy a second copy under another branch name. phenix workflow apply helloworld --follow-inject-symlinks Follow symlinks in phenix-injects/ and copy targets as regular files or directories. phenix workflow apply helloworld -c alt.yml Use another workflow config from the directory. docker exec phenix phenix workflow apply helloworld -f Run it in a Docker Compose deployment. 
# In CI, deploy a checkout under its git branch name. "/" isn't allowed in a
# workflow branch name, and the guard stops the command when BRANCH is unset
: "${BRANCH:?}" && phenix workflow apply ./site -b "${BRANCH//\//-}" -f

# Check every topology directory without changing anything
for dir in /phenix/topologies/*/; do
  phenix workflow apply "$dir" -n || echo "check $dir"
done

docs.title: Workflow Config
docs.text:
The workflow config is a phēnix config of kind Workflow. It isn't stored in phēnix; it's sent with each apply.

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v0
kind: Workflow
metadata: {}
spec:
  auto:
    create: ${BRANCH_NAME}
    update: true
    restart: true
  topology: ${BRANCH_NAME}
  scenario: ${BRANCH_NAME}
  vlans:
    EXP: 101
  schedules:
    host-01: compute1
  deployMode: all
  useGREMesh: false
  vlanRange:
    min: 100
    max: 200
  defaultBridge: phenix
Field Default Description apiVersion required phenix.sandia.gov/v0. kind required Workflow. metadata Not used today. It is accepted so a workflow config has the same top-level keys as every other phēnix config, and so a later version can add a name or annotations without a breaking change. spec required Holds the fields below; spec: {} applies every default. auto.create unset The name of the experiment to create when none is mapped to the branch. Unset never creates one. auto.update true Update the experiment mapped to the branch. A running experiment is only updated if auto.restart is also true. auto.restart true Restart a running experiment to update it, and start an experiment that was just created or updated. topology the experiment's topology The topology config to use. Required to create an experiment. scenario the experiment's scenario The scenario config to use, if any. vlans VLAN alias to VLAN ID. schedules VM hostname to cluster host. deployMode the server's deploy-mode Which minimega VMs to deploy: all, no-headnode or only-headnode. useGREMesh false Use GRE tunnels between mesh nodes for VLAN trunking. vlanRange.min, vlanRange.max 0 The lowest and highest VLAN IDs minimega may assign. 0 leaves that end unset. defaultBridge phenix The bridge VMs connect to by default: at most 15 characters and, unless it's phenix, used by no other experiment.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text: The config is validated against the Workflow schema in v0.yaml, which a running server serves at GET /api/v1/schemas/workflow/v0. An unknown or misspelled key, a value of the wrong type or a missing spec is rejected with a validation error and changes nothing.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
An experiment is mapped to a branch when its phenix.workflow/branch annotation is the branch name. phēnix sets it on the experiments a workflow creates. The server plans one action from the experiments mapped to the branch:

Mapped experiments Condition Action 0 auto.create not set none 0 auto.create set, auto.restart true createAndStart 0 auto.create set, auto.restart false create 1 auto.update false none 1 running, auto.restart false none 1 running, auto.restart true restart (needs -f in the CLI) 1 stopped, auto.restart true updateAndStart 1 stopped, auto.restart false update more than 1 any error

It is also an error when auto.create names an existing experiment that isn't mapped to the branch.

docs.title: Dry Run
docs.text:
phenix workflow apply -n asks the server to check everything the command would send, and changes nothing. A real apply runs the same checks before it changes anything, so a mistake in a config never stops a running experiment. The server checks that:

  • each config passes its schema, and each topology's nodes pass the checks an experiment start makes, such as duplicate or reserved hostnames;
  • the workflow config passes its schema;
  • the topology and scenario the workflow config names exist and, to create an experiment, that the scenario is annotated for the topology;
  • the plan has no conflict (see Actions).

A first deploy can be checked too: the topology and scenario may come from the directory's phenix-configs/ before they are stored in phēnix.

docs.title: Validation Errors
docs.text:
When a config fails schema validation, phēnix explains each error in one line:

<item> "<hostname|name>" (line N): <what> (at <sub-path>)

<item> is the list element that holds the error, such as nodes[1], with its hostname or name, and <sub-path> is the path inside it. When a missing key exists elsewhere in the same item, usually because it's indented at the wrong level, a hint: line follows.

For example, a topology where the second node's image is one level too high:

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Topology
metadata:
  name: helloworld
spec:
  nodes:
  - type: VirtualMachine
    general:
      hostname: host-01
    hardware:
      os_type: linux
      drives:
      - image: ubuntu.qc2
  - type: VirtualMachine
    general:
      hostname: host-02
    hardware:
      os_type: linux
      image: ubuntu.qc2
      drives:
      - interface: virtio

nodes[1] "host-02" (line 21): property "image" is missing (at hardware.drives[0].image)
  hint: "image:" is on line 19 under nodes[1].hardware, but the schema expects it at nodes[1].hardware.drives[0].image

These lines appear in the output of phenix workflow apply and phenix config create, in the web UI's config editor and upload dialog, and in the metadata.validation field of API errors. The validator's original text is in metadata.validation-raw.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
The command is a client of two endpoints, which CI jobs and scripts can call directly. The API docs list every parameter and status under the Workflow tag.

Endpoint Description POST /api/v1/workflow/configs/{branch} Create or update one config. POST /api/v1/workflow/apply/{branch} Apply the workflow config and return the action as JSON.

Send the file as the body, with Content-Type: application/x-yaml or application/json. When authentication is enabled, add the X-phenix-auth-token: Bearer <token> header (see API).

Query parameter Endpoint Description dryRun=true both Run every check and change nothing. pending=<ref> apply, dry run only A config you will store before the real apply; <ref> is the pending value its config dry run returned. Repeat it for more configs. expect=<action> apply Return 409 and change nothing when the server plans another action. tag=<key>=<value> apply A tag to store on the experiment. Repeat it for more tags.

This is what phenix workflow apply does, without the injects, for a directory with one topology config:

API=http://localhost:3000/api/v1/workflow
YAML='Content-Type: application/x-yaml'

# 1. Check the config
curl -sS --fail-with-body -X POST -H "$YAML" --data-binary @phenix-configs/topology.yml "$API/configs/helloworld?dryRun=true"

# 2. Plan the apply, naming the config that step 3 stores
curl -sS --fail-with-body -X POST -H "$YAML" --data-binary @phenix.yml \
  "$API/apply/helloworld?dryRun=true&pending=Topology/helloworld"

# 3. Store the config
curl -sS --fail-with-body -X POST -H "$YAML" --data-binary @phenix-configs/topology.yml "$API/configs/helloworld"

# 4. Apply, only if the plan is still the one step 2 returned
curl -sS --fail-with-body -X POST -H "$YAML" --data-binary @phenix.yml "$API/apply/helloworld?expect=createAndStart"

The apply answers with its plan:

{"action":"createAndStart","experiment":"helloworld","reason":"","dryRun":false}

On the phēnix host, the same endpoints are served on the unix socket without authentication:

curl -sS --unix-socket /tmp/phenix.sock -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/x-yaml' \
  --data-binary @phenix.yml 'http://unix/api/v1/workflow/apply/helloworld?dryRun=true'

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
With Docker Compose, the unix socket is inside the phenix container, so run the command there:

docker exec phenix phenix workflow apply helloworld -n
docker exec phenix phenix workflow apply /phenix/topologies/helloworld -f

Keep topology directories under /phenix, which is mounted at the same path in the container, and pass an absolute path or a bare name: a relative path resolves inside the container. To change a setting, set its environment variable in the phenix service and recreate the container.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Description base-dir.injects <base-dir.phenix>/injects Where injects are copied to. The server's value is used unless --base-dir.injects is given on the command line. base-dir.topologies <base-dir.phenix>/topologies Where phenix workflow apply NAME looks for NAME.

Use absolute paths for both. See the Settings Reference for how to set them.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The command only works on the phēnix host or in the phēnix container. A CI job on another machine can call the REST API, but has to get the injects onto the phēnix host itself.
  • There is no web UI for workflow apply.
  • Avoid sending workflow requests for different branches at the same moment: the server sets BRANCH_NAME for the whole process while it parses a request.
  • A dry run can't find every error. It doesn't merge the topologies that a not yet stored topology includes, and it checks only the schema of an Experiment config. The real apply can then fail after the injects are copied and the configs stored, but before any experiment has changed.
  • Don't add an Experiment config named like the workflow's auto.create to phenix-configs/; let auto.create create the experiment.
  • Grant the workflow:create permission only to trusted roles: an apply dry run can reveal whether a file exists on the server.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Permission denied. Your user may not write to the unix socket or to the injects directory. Run the command as the user that runs phenix ui, usually root (with Docker Compose, through docker exec), or start phenix ui with --unix-socket-gid set to the ID of a group you are in.
  • The server doesn't answer. Check that phenix ui is running and listens on the socket that --unix-socket names, /tmp/phenix.sock by default.
  • The server is refused. The server is from another phēnix release than the CLI; use the same release for both.
  • The run stops and asks for -f. The plan would restart a running experiment. Nothing was changed; run it again with -f to allow it.
  • The plan changed (409). The experiment was started or stopped between the plan and apply steps. Run the command again.
  • The injects destination is refused. The destination overlaps a topology directory, or the server reports a relative base-dir.injects. Check base-dir.injects and -b.
  • A run stopped after it changed something. A run that stops in or after injects leaves the injects and the configs it stored in place, and its error says what was changed. Fix the cause and run the command again. Only a run that stops in apply can have changed the experiment.
  • Leftovers next to the injects. Hidden .<name>.tmp-* and .<name>.old-* entries in <base-dir.injects> are left by an interrupted run. Remove them by hand when no other run is active.
  • No commit tag. Git refuses a repository that another user owns, which is common under docker exec. Add the directory to git's safe.directory for the user that runs the command.
  • No output. With log.level at warn or higher, the plan and the result aren't printed; rely on the exit status.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• Server check. In preflight the command reads GET /api/v1/options from the unix socket. The server must report "workflow-dry-run": true: an older server would store configs during a dry run. The answer also carries the server's base-dir.injects.
  • Pending configs. In plan, each config's dry run returns a pending ref such as Topology/helloworld. The workflow config's dry run sends these refs, so the server plans as if the configs were stored and checks the references between them.
  • Injects. phenix-injects/ is copied to a temporary directory next to <base-dir.injects>/<name> and swapped into place, so a failed copy leaves the previous copy intact. Symbolic links are copied as links, and only permission bits are kept.
  • Apply. The real apply sends expect=<the planned action>, so the server changes nothing when the plan differs from the one that was checked.

docs.title: Builder
docs.text: Builder is the graphical topology editor of the phēnix Web-UI. You draw devices, switches and connections on a canvas, and when you publish, Builder writes the Topology config for you.

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
• Draw a diagram: devices, switches, connections, groups, notes and drawings, with your own colors and icons. A switch is one network.
  • Import a stored Topology or Experiment config, or a config file, as a new draft. Upload a file that is already a diagram, for example from another phēnix server.
  • Arrange the diagram with one of five automatic layouts, or by hand.
  • Add devices from templates, kept in the diagram or in a library that all users share.
  • Check the diagram while you work. Builder marks an interface with no VLAN, two devices with one hostname, and other issues before you publish.
  • Publish the diagram as a Topology config, and optionally an Experiment config with one of its scenarios.
  • Go back. Builder saves each change to the server, and Draft History restores an earlier snapshot.
  • Download the diagram as a PNG or SVG picture, a draw.io file, a Gephi (GEXF) file, or a Topology YAML file.
  • Work from the keyboard alone, with a command palette and shortcuts.

docs.title: How Builder fits phēnix
docs.text:
A diagram lives in a draft on the phēnix server. Drafts are separate from configs: the Configs page does not list them, and a change to a draft writes no config. Only Publish writes a Topology or Experiment config from the draft. Until then, you can draw, check and change as much as you want.

A published topology names its diagram. On the Configs page it has the tag builder, and the tag opens the diagram in Builder again. An experiment runs from the Topology config, not from the diagram.

The diagram holds more than the topology: positions, groups, notes, colors, icons and layers. Publishing leaves them out. A Builder JSON download keeps them.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
Click Builder in the navigation bar to open it.

  1. Do the Tutorial. It takes about 10 minutes and ends with a published topology and an experiment.
  2. Read the page of the feature that you need. The feature pages are Drafts, The Editor, Diagrams, Templates and Icons, Import, Upload and Download and Publishing.
  3. When something does not work, see Troubleshooting. Messages, codes, shortcuts and limits are in the Reference.

Each feature page ends with links into its details page, which holds every rule, limit and message of the feature.

Note

Earlier phēnix releases had a different graphical editor, also named Builder. Builder converts its diagrams when you import or upload them: see Legacy Builder.

docs.title: Administration
docs.text: This page is for phēnix administrators. Every phēnix server has Builder, and roles control who can use it.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The permission builder use gives a user Builder. With it, a user reads and changes every draft and the three libraries. Drafts have no owner. A draft records who created and last changed it, for information only.

To give a role Builder, add this policy to it:

- resources:
  - builder
  verbs:
  - use

The policy takes no resource names. builder use gives no access to configs. With authentication disabled, all users work as global-admin. Of the built-in roles, only Global Admin and Builder have builder use.

docs.title: The Builder role
docs.text:
The built-in role Builder is for users who draw diagrams and publish them as topologies. It holds:

  • builder use.
  • configs list, get, create, update and delete, on Topology/*, Scenario/* and Experiment/* only.
  • schemas get, topologies and scenarios list and get, experiments list, get, create and update, and disks list.

Each time phenix ui starts, it makes sure that the role exists and has builder use. It changes no other role. Add the builder policy to each other role that must use Builder. Then assign roles on the Users page (see Users).

docs.title: What each task needs
docs.text:
builder use alone allows all work on drafts, the libraries, the Inspector fields, and Upload of a Builder document. Other tasks also need configs permissions:

  • An import of a stored config needs get on the config, and topologies or experiments list on its name.
  • An import of a config file needs get and create.
  • A publish needs create or update on each config that it writes.
  • Preflight needs the permissions of each check.

What each task needs lists every task.

docs.title: Example role
docs.text:
The example role Topology Designer cannot publish, import a config file or delete a topology. It also cannot store a scenario file or create the configs of a package. It can do all other work on drafts and the libraries. A user with the Builder role can then publish its drafts. To add the role:

  1. Download topology-designer.role.yaml.
  2. Store it with phenix config create.
  3. Assign it on the Users page.

Warning

Do not use "*/*" in the configs policy of a role. It also matches User and Role configs, so a user could read password hashes.

phēnix copies the policies of a role into a user when you assign the role. After you change a Role config, assign the role to its users again.

docs.title: What users without a permission see
docs.text: Builder hides or disables each control that the role does not allow, and the server checks each request. Without builder use, the navigation bar has no Builder link, and /builder says "Your role does not include the Builder." Without configs update, the command palette says "Your role cannot publish diagrams." Without disks list, the checks say that Builder does not check drive images.

docs.title: The libraries
docs.text: The server keeps one template library, one layer set library and one icon library, which all Builder users share and change. No role can change the built-in templates, the server collections, the built-in layer set Purdue Model, or the icons that phēnix added from template files. Duplicate makes a copy of a read-only template or layer set that users can change. phēnix logs each library change with the user name (see The libraries).

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Drafts, published documents and the libraries are records in the phēnix store, not configs. phenix config list and the Configs page do not list them. The limits are in Limits.

When phēnix starts, and each hour, it deletes the published documents that no topology references. It also deletes the stored documents that no draft and no published document names. Clean up… in the Builder settings does the same at once, and also deletes each draft with no change since its last publish. It shows what it would delete and asks before it deletes (see Cleaning up storage).

docs.title: Template files on the server
docs.text:
To give all users the same node templates, put template files in the template directory of the server. When phenix ui starts, it reads each file as one read-only collection. A file has the format that the Node Templates tab downloads (see the example node-templates.yaml).

The directory is <base-dir.phenix>/builder/templates, by default /phenix/builder/templates. To change it, set base-dir.builder-templates with the flag --base-dir.builder-templates, the environment variable PHENIX_BASE_DIR_BUILDER_TEMPLATES, or the config file (see Settings):

base-dir:
  builder-templates: /etc/phenix/builder-templates

phēnix reads the files directly in the directory that end in .yaml, .yml or .json (see Limits). It skips a file that is not valid and logs a warning. It reads the directory only when it starts, so restart phenix ui after you add, change or delete a file. phēnix adds the custom icons of a file to the icon library as server icons, when the library does not have them. No user can rename or delete a server icon (see Template files on the server).

docs.title: The builder-doc annotation
docs.text:
A topology names its diagram in the builder-doc annotation of its Topology config. The annotation is a map with up to three keys: digest, id and path. Publish writes digest and id. You write path yourself, for a Builder file. A topology shows the published document that the annotation names, or else the file at path, or else none (see Which diagram a topology shows).

phēnix checks the annotation each time anyone creates or updates a Topology config, and refuses a config whose annotation is not valid (see The builder-doc annotation). After a rename, or a copy of the config, phēnix deletes the id. Without a path, it deletes the whole annotation (see Renaming and copying a topology).

docs.title: A Builder file beside a topology
docs.text:
A topology in a repository can keep its diagram there, as a Builder JSON or YAML file. Name the file in the annotation:

apiVersion: phenix.sandia.gov/v1
kind: Topology
metadata:
  name: pump-station
  annotations:
    builder-doc:
      path: /phenix/topologies/pump-station/pump-station.builder.json

To make such a config:

  1. Open the draft in Builder, or upload the Builder file.
  2. Click Download > Topology YAML.
  3. Set metadata.name.
  4. Add the annotation. Do not change the spec.
  5. Store the config with phenix config create.

The Published Diagrams tab then lists the topology with the tag File. phēnix reads the file each time someone opens the diagram, so a git pull that changes the file changes the diagram. phēnix reads a file only when all of these are true:

  • The file is below the base directory, /phenix or the base-dir.phenix setting.
  • It is outside the VM mount directory.
  • It is a regular file within the size limit in Limits.
  • It holds one valid Builder document.

Otherwise, opening the diagram fails with "Could not open the diagram of topology pump-station." and a sentence that names the path (see When the file cannot be used).

Warning

The name of a topology does not protect its Builder file. A user who has configs get, and create or update, on any one topology name can store a topology there with any path below the base directory. The user can then open that file. Keep a Builder file below the base directory only when each such user may read it. See Who can read a Builder file.

To accept one document only, add digest beside path. The digest is the SHA-256 of the document as phēnix writes it, which the REST API gives (see Pinning the file with a digest).

Publish never writes the file. It stores a published document and writes digest and id beside the path. The file is out of date until you replace it with Download > Builder JSON (see Editing and publishing).

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
Scripts use the same REST API as the Web-UI, under /api/v1. The interactive API docs of a running server, at /docs/, describe each route under the Builder tag (see API).

Each route needs builder use, and a route that reads or writes configs also needs the configs permissions of the Web-UI task. With authentication enabled, send a token in the X-Phenix-Auth-Token header as Bearer <token>. A refused request answers with a JSON body whose code names the failure (see Errors of the REST API). The route table and examples are in REST API.

docs.title: More detail
docs.text:
• Administration: details: every permission, limit, store record, file rule and REST route.
  • Troubleshooting and Troubleshooting: details: what a message means, and what to do.
  • Availability, Response headers and Compressed files: the Content-Security-Policy that a proxy must allow, the response headers, and PHENIX_BROTLI_QUALITY.
  • Users and Settings: roles, tokens and the base-dir settings.

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text: This page shows how to draw a diagram, with the Riverside Water draft of the example lab as the example. Keep one idea in mind: a switch is one network, and a connection puts an interface on that network.

docs.title: What a diagram is
docs.text:
A diagram describes one Topology config. Publishing writes only some of its parts:

In the diagram In the Topology config A device A node in spec.nodes, with its settings A switch A network, whose name is the VLAN of its interfaces A connection An interface with the network's name as its vlan A device from an included topology Nothing. includeTopologies names that topology Notes, groups, drawings, colors, icons, layers and templates Nothing

docs.title: Add devices
docs.text:
Nodes & Objects, in the left column, lists what you can add. Click an item, or drag it to the canvas. Or press Ctrl+K (⌘+K on macOS) and select Add device in the command palette. Device has default settings. The five built-in templates under Templates set more fields (see Built-in templates and Templates and Icons).

The vrouter app configures a device of type Router or Firewall. An external device is hardware, such as a PLC. phēnix starts no VM for it, and its interfaces tell phēnix which VLANs the hardware is on (see External Nodes).

docs.title: Networks
docs.text:
A switch is one network. To add one:

  1. Click Switch under Nodes & Objects.
  2. In the Inspector, set Name.
  3. Click Apply.

When you rename a network, the VLAN of each interface on it changes.

A network has these optional fields:

  • VLAN alias, from 1 to 4094. When you publish with an experiment, it goes into vlans.aliases.
  • Subnet, such as 10.1.0.0/24.
  • Gateway.

With a subnet, each static interface that you connect gets the next free host address and the subnet's Mask. This needs the Assign addresses on connect setting, which is on by default. If the interface has no Gateway of its own, it also gets the network's gateway.

Assign addresses gives addresses to the static interfaces that have none. Builder never changes an address that an interface has.

A new network gets a suggested subnet, which you can change or clear (see Subnets and addresses).

docs.title: Connect an interface
docs.text:
A connection puts an interface on a network. To connect ws-03 to CORP:

  • Drag from the + handle under ws-03, or from an unconnected connection point on its side, to the CORP switch. A drag from + adds a new static interface.
  • Select ws-03. Click Add connection in the Inspector header. Select the switch CORP (CORP), then click Connect.
  • In the Inspector, click Add interface under Network. Enter Address 10.10.20.103 and VLAN CORP, then click Apply.

CORP has no subnet, so enter the address of eth0 in the Inspector, or give CORP a subnet first. A VLAN that names a network connects the interface to that network's switch. A VLAN that names no network leaves the interface unconnected, and a typed VLAN gives no address.

To disconnect an interface, do one of these steps:

  • Click Disconnect next to the interface under Connection points in the Inspector.
  • Select the connection and press Delete (⌫ on macOS).

The interface stays with no VLAN and blocks publishing.

Hide connections in the command palette hides the connections on your canvas only (see Hiding connections).

docs.title: Edit device settings
docs.text:
Change the fields of a device in the Inspector or the Node Editor, then click Apply (see The Editor). Interface kind is Static or OSPF, DHCP or manual or Serial. A new interface is Static or OSPF with Mask 24. When you change the kind, Builder asks first, and Switch and clear empties the interface.

Routes and Firewall rulesets are under Network, and the vrouter app applies them when the experiment starts. Labels and annotations are under More settings, and Builder reads an annotation value as YAML. When your role can list the server's disk images, a drive's Image suggests them (see Drive images).

To duplicate a device, select it, then press Ctrl+D (⌘+D on macOS). The copy, such as historian-01-2, keeps every setting but not its connections. The header says 1 warning until you give the copy its own hostname and address, and connect it.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
A note is text on the canvas, and publishing ignores it. To add one:

  1. Click Note under Nodes & Objects.
  2. In the Inspector, enter the Text.
  3. Click Apply.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
A group is a box with a title around nodes, and publishing ignores it. When you move a group, its nodes move with it. To group nodes:

  1. Select the first node. Then hold Shift and select the others.
  2. Click Group in the toolbar, or press Ctrl+G (⌘+G on macOS).

Ungroup keeps the nodes and deletes the group. Its key is Ctrl+Shift+G (⇧+⌘+G on macOS). A node that you drag onto a group does not go into it. Click Move to group in the Inspector header instead.

Auto-group in the toolbar puts nodes into new groups:

  • By network: each network's switch with its devices.
  • By name: devices whose hostnames share a stem, such as web-01 and web-02.
  • By name pattern…: nodes whose names match a regular expression (see Grouping by a name pattern).

docs.title: Drawings
docs.text: Rectangles, circles, icons and lines are drawings. Publishing ignores them, and they take no connections. Add one under Nodes & Objects, then set its fields, such as Label, in the Inspector. A line also has a Line style, arrowhead fields and 2 to 64 Points (see Shapes, icons and lines).

docs.title: Colors, line styles and icon size
docs.text:
Switches, connections, devices, notes, groups, shapes and lines have color fields in the Inspector. Edge Color of a switch colors its network: its connections and switch outlines. Outline Color and Fill Color of a device or a switch take only a hex color, such as #2f6fbf. Enter a color, or click the swatch button before the field (see Colors).

Line style, on a network or on one connection, is Auto, Solid, Dashed, Dotted or Dash-dot. Auto selects a pattern by the network's place in the diagram, so that networks differ without color.

Icon size in the Diagram section of the Inspector draws icons at Small, Medium or Large, and a device, a switch or a group can have its own. Two settings change your canvas only: every icon at one size, or no icons (see Your own icon size and hidden icons).

docs.title: Icons
docs.text: Select the icon of a device, a group or an icon drawing under Icon in the Inspector. The icon is only a picture and changes no setting (see Built-in icons). To show your own image, select Custom icon… at the end of the list. Then upload an image file, or click Use on an icon of the server (see Templates and Icons).

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
A layer has an ID, from 0 to 99, and a label, and can have an icon, a color and node matchers. A device or a switch can be at one layer. Layers are for the picture only, and an import sets none. A diagram with no layers of its own has 7 placeholder layers (see Placeholder layers).

To set the layer of a device or a switch, select it. Then select a layer under Layer in the Inspector. A node matcher puts a device at a layer by its fields, for example hostnames that start with plc- (see Node matchers). A layer's color can also outline its nodes (see Layer outlines). Edit layers… under Layer opens the layers editor, with a row for each layer and Add layer.

docs.title: Layer sets
docs.text: A layer set is a list of layers in the server's library. In the layers editor, Use a layer set gives the diagram a linked copy of a set. Save to layer set saves your changes as the set's next version. Set default on the Layers tab of the drafts page gives each new blank diagram that set (see Layer sets).

docs.title: Example: the Purdue model
docs.text:
The built-in layer set Purdue Model gives each Purdue level a layer, from "L5 Enterprise" (ID 6) to "L0 Process" (ID 0). See Purdue Model layer set. To use it:

  1. Open the layers editor.
  2. Select Purdue Model (built-in) under Use a layer set.
  3. Click Apply.

In Lakeside Water Treatment, each device and switch is at the layer of its Purdue level. To try it, upload lakeside-treatment.builder.json, then select By layer in the layout menu.

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text:
The layout menu in the toolbar arranges the whole diagram.

Layout What it does Network cards A card for each network, the switch above its devices. ELK layered Clusters each network's switch with its devices, left to right. By layer Puts the layers from top to bottom. Dagre Devices beside their switch, networks along the connections. Standard Every device in a row above the switches.

ELK layered suits most diagrams. Layouts keep groups together. Right after a layout runs, the menu offers Restore previous layout.

By layer puts the highest layer ID at the top. For nodes with no layer, see By layer.

docs.title: Arrange by hand
docs.text: Drag a node, or several selected nodes. Press Shift with an arrow key to move them 10 pixels. Or enter X and Y under Position in the Inspector, then click Move. The Snap to grid setting, off by default, puts the nodes that you drag or add on the grid (see The grid).

docs.title: Copy, paste, duplicate and delete
docs.text: Copy, Paste and Delete are in the toolbar, and Duplicate is in the command palette. Copy and Paste work between drafts that you open in the same browser tab. Builder pastes a connection only with both of its nodes, so copy a device with its switch. When you delete a device, Builder also deletes its connections.

docs.title: Undo and redo
docs.text: Undo and Redo in the toolbar go back and forward through your changes. They reach only the changes since you opened the draft in this tab. To go back further, use Draft History (see Drafts and Undo and redo).

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
A diagram lists up to 20 Scenario configs, and an experiment published with the topology uses one of them (see Publishing). To add the stored scenario riverside-water:

  1. Click Scenarios in the toolbar.
  2. Under Scenarios of this diagram, select the checkbox of riverside-water.
  3. Click Save scenarios.

The dialog lists the server's scenarios that your role can list. A checkbox adds one to the diagram's list, and the scenario on the server does not change. View shows a scenario as read-only YAML, and Edit opens it in a text field, where Save scenario replaces the stored scenario. Create new scenario and Upload a scenario (YAML or JSON) store a scenario on the server (see Scenarios).

docs.title: Included topologies
docs.text:
riverside-water includes the topology corp-services, so dns-01 and ntp-01 are in the diagram, with a dashed border and the text "Included from corp-services". You can move them, but their fields are read only. You cannot delete or connect them, delete their connections, or rename their network, CORP. To change dns-01, change corp-services, then import riverside-water again.

To change included devices in the diagram itself, select one, then click Combine into a new draft in the Inspector. A new draft, Riverside-Water-combined, opens with them as normal devices, and publishing it makes a new topology (see Making included devices editable).

docs.title: More detail
docs.text:
• Building a Diagram: details: every rule, limit and message.
  • Layers: details, Icons: details and Scenarios and Included Topologies: details.
  • Node matchers: fields and patterns for layers.
  • Layouts: each layout, and the layouts of earlier versions.
  • Limits: the limits of layers, patterns, icons and scenarios.

docs.title: Drafts
docs.text: A draft is a diagram saved on the phēnix server, with its history. Builder saves each change that you make, and only Publish writes a config.

docs.title: The drafts page
docs.text:
The drafts page opens when you click Builder in the navigation bar.

At the top right, Blank diagram, Import and Upload start a new draft. Commands opens the command palette. The shortcut is Ctrl+K (⌘+K on macOS). For the other buttons, see Top right buttons.

The five tabs are Drafts, Published Diagrams, Node Templates, Layers and Icons. Templates and Icons describes templates and icons.

The Drafts tab lists the drafts of all users, most recently changed first. Each Builder user can open, change and delete each draft. A card shows the name, the creator and the last change, with Open, Duplicate, Delete and Publish. Publish opens the Publish diagram dialog without the editor (see Publishing from the drafts page and Item buttons).

To find a draft, enter part of its name or a user name in Filter drafts (see Filtering the lists).

docs.title: Create a draft
docs.text:
• Blank diagram opens a new draft named "Untitled topology".
  • Import makes a draft from a Topology or Experiment config, stored in phēnix or in a file.
  • Upload makes a draft from a Builder JSON or YAML file, pasted text, a published diagram, or a legacy Builder diagram. See Import, Upload and Download and Legacy Builder.
  • Edit as a draft makes a draft from a published diagram (see The Published Diagrams tab). The tag builder on the Configs page does the same.

docs.title: Open a draft
docs.text:
Click Open on the draft card. Or use the command palette:

  1. Press Ctrl+K.
  2. Enter open draft and press Enter.
  3. Enter part of the name and press Enter.

To go back to the list, click Drafts in the editor header. While a draft is open, the address bar shows its link, which works for each Builder user (see Links to a draft).

docs.title: How drafts save
docs.text:
Builder saves each change to the server as you make it. There is no Save button. The save state in the toolbar shows where your changes are, for example All changes saved (see Save states). Save now sends the changes at once. The shortcut is Ctrl+S (⌘+S on macOS).

When Builder cannot reach the server, it keeps your changes in this browser, and you can continue to edit. The save state then shows Retry saving. Builder sends the changes within a few seconds after the server answers again, or when you click Retry saving. See Working offline.

docs.title: Draft History
docs.text:
Each saved change is a snapshot. Draft History in the toolbar lists the snapshots, newest first. Current marks the current snapshot.

To go back to an earlier snapshot, click Restore in its row. Restoring does not delete the newer snapshots.

Warning

A change after a restore or an undo deletes all newer snapshots. This includes the snapshots of other users.

While the draft shows an older snapshot, a notice above the toolbar says how many newer snapshots your next change deletes. Return to latest shows the newest snapshot again. Save newer history as a new draft makes a new draft of the newest snapshot, and you stay on this draft (see Newer snapshots).

To delete a snapshot, click Delete in its row. Then click Delete snapshot. You cannot undo this. You cannot delete the current snapshot.

Sometimes the Inspector has changes that you did not apply. If you then leave, publish or download the draft, Builder applies and saves these changes. The snapshot has the mark Automatic.

Undo and Redo also move the current snapshot, one change at a time. They skip a deleted snapshot (see Undo and redo).

docs.title: Duplicate a draft
docs.text: Duplicate on a card makes a new draft with a copy of the current diagram, and opens it. The copy has "(copy)" after its name, no history, and no link to a topology or experiment. When you publish it, Builder asks for a new topology name and makes a new topology (see Duplicating a draft).

docs.title: Delete a draft
docs.text:
1. Click Delete on the draft card.
  2. Click Delete draft.

Builder deletes the draft and its history from the server. You cannot undo this. The configs that the draft published do not change.

docs.title: Select several drafts
docs.text:
Each draft card has a checkbox. The row above the cards shows the number of selected cards, Select all, Download selected and Delete selected.

  • Download selected saves a Builder JSON file for each selected draft.
  • Delete selected asks once for all the drafts. A summary under the row lists the drafts that Builder could not delete.

You can also select cards with the keyboard (see Selecting with the keyboard).

docs.title: The Published Diagrams tab
docs.text:
The Published Diagrams tab lists each topology that has a Builder diagram. Open on a card shows the diagram read only.

To change the diagram, click Edit as a draft. Builder makes a draft from the published diagram and opens it. If a draft already published this diagram, or was made from it, Edit as a draft opens that draft instead. The draft can publish to the topology again (see Publishing).

When Builder published a diagram with an experiment, its card and the editor toolbar have Exp, which opens the experiment page (see Opening the experiment).

A card with the tag File is a topology whose diagram comes from a Builder file on the server. It has no Delete (see Diagrams read from a file). On the other cards, Delete deletes the Topology config from phēnix. The drafts and experiments made from it do not change (see Deleting a published topology).

docs.title: The Layers tab
docs.text:
A layer set is a named list of layers and its options (see Diagrams). The Layers tab lists the layer set library, which all users share. The built-in set Purdue Model has the seven levels of the Purdue model, from L0 Process to L5 Enterprise. To change it, click Duplicate. Then change the copy.

Set default makes a set the default set of the server. Each Blank diagram starts with a copy of the default set (see The Layers tab and Selecting several layer sets).

docs.title: Damaged drafts
docs.text: A draft that this phēnix server cannot read stays on the list, with Delete but no Open. See Damaged drafts.

docs.title: Logging out
docs.text: Logging out deletes the unsent changes from the browser. Before you log out, wait until the save state says All changes saved. See Logging out.

docs.title: The same draft in two tabs
docs.text: Do not open one draft in more than one tab. When you do, each tab shows a notice. When both tabs hold unsaved changes, Builder can save the changes of only one tab. See Same draft in multiple tabs.

docs.title: Draft merging
docs.text: Another user can save a newer version of the draft before your changes reach the server. Builder then merges their changes with yours, field by field. When a change clashes, Builder shows This draft changed on the server, and you select the changes to keep. See Draft merging.

docs.title: The draft limit
docs.text: At its draft limit, the server refuses new drafts. To make space, delete drafts, or click Clean up… in Settings. See Limits.

docs.title: More detail
docs.text:
• Drafts: details: every rule and message.
  • Save states: every save state message.
  • Draft limits: the draft and snapshot limits.

docs.title: The Editor
docs.text: In the editor, you draw and change a diagram, and Builder saves each change and checks the diagram while you work. This page explains the parts of the editor, the checks, the command palette and the settings.

docs.title: The five areas
docs.text: The editor has five areas: the header, the toolbar, Nodes & Objects at the left, the canvas, and the Inspector at the right.

docs.title: Header
docs.text:
From left to right, the header holds:

  • Drafts, which opens the drafts page.
  • The diagram name, with Edit diagram name (the pencil), except in a published diagram.
  • The resource totals of the devices that phēnix starts (see Resource totals).
  • The counts of devices, switches, networks, connections, groups and notes. Click a count to select all items of that kind (see Selecting by kind).
  • The checks button: No issues, or a count such as 3 warnings.
  • The view buttons: Reset view, Commands, the theme button, Shortcuts, Settings, Help and Focus mode.

To rename the diagram:

  1. Click Edit diagram name. A field replaces the name.
  2. Enter the new name.
  3. Press Enter.

The topology name is different: you enter it when you publish (see Publishing).

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
• Undo, Redo: undo or redo the last change.
  • Copy, Paste, Delete: copy, paste or delete the selection.
  • Group, Ungroup, Auto-group: put the selected nodes in a new group, delete a selected group and keep its nodes, or group by network or by name.
  • The layout menu: arrange the diagram.
  • Scenarios: select, view, edit or create the scenarios.
  • Download, Upload: save the diagram as a file, or open a diagram file as a new draft.
  • Publish, Exp: write the configs, or open the experiment that you published. Exp shows only while that experiment exists and your role can read it.
  • Minimap, Draft History: show or hide the minimap, or restore a snapshot of the draft.

The save state follows, for example All changes saved. When a save fails, Retry saving follows it (see Drafts). A button whose action can take time shows a turning ring (see Actions that take time).

docs.title: Canvas
docs.text:
• To select: click a node or a connection. Shift+click adds a node to the selection, or deselects it. Click an empty spot to clear the selection.
  • To move: drag a node.
  • To pan: drag an empty spot.
  • To zoom: use the mouse wheel, or the zoom buttons at the bottom left.
  • To connect: drag from the connection point of a device to a switch (see Diagrams).

The minimap at the bottom right shows the full diagram. Reset view in the header resets the zoom, the minimap and the side columns, and does not change the diagram (see Canvas).

Rest the pointer on a device or a switch to see its info tooltip (see Info tooltips).

docs.title: Side columns
docs.text:
You can widen, hide or resize the left column and the Inspector at the right (see Side columns). The buttons for the left column use the name Nodes & Templates.

Nodes & Objects lists Device, Switch, Note, Group and the drawings. Click an item to add it, or drag it onto the canvas. Templates lists the device templates (see Templates and Icons).

docs.title: Inspector
docs.text:
The Inspector shows and changes the fields of one selected node or connection. With nothing selected, or with several items selected, it shows the diagram:

  • Name and Description. Click Apply to keep a change.
  • Layers: Edit layers… opens the layers editor.
  • Notes: text about the full diagram.
  • Scenarios: Edit scenarios opens the Scenarios dialog (see Diagrams).

For the other fields, see With nothing selected.

docs.title: Editing a node
docs.text:
Select a node to see its fields. A device has Hostname, Icon and the colors at the top, then the sections Node, Hardware, Network, More settings, Layer, Connection points and Position.

A field marked * must have a value. A field with a value other than its default shows a Default button.

To change fields:

  1. Change one or more fields. A bar at the bottom says "Unapplied changes", with Apply and Cancel.
  2. Click Apply, or press Enter in a field. Builder changes the diagram and saves it.

Cancel discards the changes. While a changed field has an error, Apply is unavailable. When you select another node, the Inspector applies valid changes and discards changes that are not valid. Icon, the colors and Layer take effect at once, without Apply (see Fields that take effect at once).

Icon opens the list of built-in icons. Default is the icon of the node when it has no icon of its own. Custom icon… opens the Custom icons dialog (see Templates and Icons).

You cannot change a device from an included topology, but you can move it. You cannot rename a network that an included device is on. In a published diagram, you cannot change any field (see Fields you cannot change).

With one node selected, the Inspector header has Add connection, Move to group and Open Node Editor (see The Inspector header). Click the name of a section to collapse or expand it (see Collapsing sections). The eye button beside Description hides it on the canvas (see Hiding descriptions on the canvas).

A switch, a note, a group, a connection and a drawing have their own fields (see Other kinds of nodes). A switch also has Subnet, Gateway and Assign addresses (see Addresses of a network).

docs.title: Node Editor
docs.text:
The Node Editor shows the fields of one node in a large dialog, with the checks of the node. To open it, double-click the node, or click Open Node Editor in the Inspector header.

Search fields finds a field by its label, such as memory, or by its YAML path in the Topology config, such as network.interfaces[0].vlan. Only the matching fields show. To show all fields again, empty the box.

Click Apply to apply all changes as one step of Undo and close the Node Editor. Cancel closes it. Builder asks before it discards unapplied changes. See also Sections and the table of contents and Searching the fields.

docs.title: Checks and warnings
docs.text:
Builder checks the diagram while you edit it. The canvas marks each node and connection with an issue: a cross for an error, or a triangle for only warnings.

To fix an issue:

  1. Click the checks button. The Diagram checks dialog lists the errors, then the warnings.
  2. Click Go to beside the issue. The canvas selects its node, and the Inspector shows it.
  3. Fix the field.

An error stops publishing until you fix it. Some warnings also block Publish, and the dialog says so (see Publishing). Other warnings do not block publishing.

Some issues have a Fix button. Undo reverts each fix as one step (see Fixing an issue in one step).

Builder also warns about settings that phēnix accepts but does not apply as the diagram shows them (see Rulesets and addresses and Device settings).

docs.title: Preflight
docs.text:
Preflight, at the bottom of Diagram checks, asks the phēnix server to check the saved draft against the server and its cluster. The checks write nothing and start no VM or experiment. There are four: Host capacity, Networks, Disk images and Scenario apps.

To run Preflight:

  1. Click the checks button in the header.
  2. Under Preflight, tick the checks.
  3. Optional: in Experiment (optional), enter the name of the experiment.
  4. Click Run. Builder first saves your latest changes.

Each check shows Passed, Failed or Unavailable. Unavailable means that Builder could not do all of the check, for example without a permission or a connection to minimega (see Preflight).

docs.title: Command palette
docs.text:
The command palette runs commands and finds nodes, networks, templates and icons. To open it, click Commands in the header, or press Ctrl+K (⌘+K on macOS).

  • Type words to find commands, for example layout.
  • Type @ to find a node by its hostname, address, VLAN, label or description (see Finding nodes).
  • Type # to find a network by its name or VLAN alias.
  • Type t: for node templates, c: for template collections and i: for custom icons (see Finding templates, collections and icons).
  • Type ? to see all prefixes.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text:
To see all shortcuts, click Shortcuts in the header, or press ? outside a text field. The keys that you use most are Ctrl+Z (⌘+Z on macOS) for Undo and Ctrl+D (⌘+D on macOS) for Duplicate. Delete deletes the selection, and N adds a device.

Most keys do nothing while focus is in a text field. The full table, with the macOS keys, is in the Reference. For the canvas keys, see Keys on the canvas.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: To open Builder settings, click Settings in the header, or press Alt+Shift+S (⌥+⇧+S on macOS). Changes apply at once. The settings belong to this browser: it keeps them after you log out, and they do not change the diagram. For each setting and its default, see Settings.

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
• Single-key shortcuts: ?, N and the zoom keys work without Ctrl. If speech input or your screen reader can press them by mistake, disable the setting. See Single-key shortcuts.
  • Change shortcuts, in the shortcuts sheet, gives any command other keys, or no keys. See Customizing shortcuts.
  • Clean up…, under Storage in Builder settings, deletes the published, unchanged drafts of all users and the stored data that nothing uses. It asks before it deletes. See Administration.
  • The layers editor changes the layers of the open diagram. Edit layers… opens it from the Inspector, the Node Editor, Builder settings or the command palette. See Diagrams and Layers editor.
  • Focus mode hides the phēnix navigation bar, so Builder fills the window. Click Focus mode in the header, or press Ctrl+Shift+F (⇧+⌘+F on macOS). See Focus mode.
  • The theme button in the header shows System, Light or Dark, and each click selects the next theme. The theme changes only Builder, not the rest of phēnix. See Themes.
  • Accessibility: you can use Builder with only a keyboard, and with a screen reader. Builder aims to meet WCAG 2.2 level AA. See Accessibility.

docs.title: More detail
docs.text:
• The Editor: details: every rule, limit and message.
  • Checks and Preflight: details: every check, fix and preflight result.
  • Command Palette and Shortcuts: details: every command, search prefix and key.
  • Codes: the code of each issue.
  • What blocks publishing: the warnings that Publish lists as errors.

docs.title: Import, Upload and Download
docs.text:
Builder uses three words for three tasks:

  • Import makes a draft from a Topology or Experiment config, stored in phēnix or in a file.
  • Upload opens a file that is already a diagram as a new draft. The file can be a Builder document, a Builder package, a published diagram or a legacy Builder diagram.
  • Download saves the open diagram as a file, in one of seven formats or as a Builder package.

None of these tasks changes a config. In the Web-UI, only Publish writes configs (see Publishing).

docs.title: Import a stored topology
docs.text:
1. On the drafts page, click Import.
  2. Keep Source set to Stored config and Source kind set to Topology.
  3. In Source name, select riverside-water. The dialog shows Included topologies, because riverside-water includes corp-services.
  4. Click Import. The dialog shows 1 warning: the 2 devices from corp-services are read only.
  5. Click Continue to editor.

The draft has the name of the config. An import without warnings opens the editor at once. Cancel makes no draft.

docs.title: Import an experiment
docs.text:
Set Source kind to Experiment. In Source name, select the experiment, for example riverside. An imported experiment differs from an imported topology:

  • The draft lists the scenario of the experiment, when your role can list it, but never keeps the copy in the experiment.
  • The VLAN aliases of the experiment become the VLAN alias of each network.
  • The import does not keep the VLAN range, or experiment fields such as baseDir, and warns about them.
  • The import does not keep the files that experiment apps injected into VMs at start, and does not warn about them. It keeps the injections of the topology.

The import also removes the values that phēnix added when it created the experiment (see Importing an experiment).

docs.title: Import a config file
docs.text:
1. Click Import.
  2. Set Source to Config file.
  3. In Topology or Experiment config, choose the file, for example pump-station.topology.yaml. The file can be JSON or YAML, up to 5 MiB.
  4. Click Import.

A draft from a config file can only publish a new topology, also when a stored config has the same name. Builder keeps each ${NAME} and ${NAME:default} in the file as written. Unlike phenix config create, it never replaces them with values from the environment of the server. Edit such a value in the draft before you publish (see Importing a config file).

docs.title: Import options
docs.text:
When the topology includes other topologies, the dialog offers:

  • Keep included nodes read only, the default. You cannot change the included nodes in the draft, and publishing keeps the includes.
  • Combine into one new topology. The import copies the included nodes into the diagram as ordinary devices, and publishing creates a new topology.

Create a new topology as a copy shows for a stored topology when you do not combine. With a copy or a combined import, New topology name proposes the source name with -copy or -combined. Such a draft is not linked to the source topology and cannot update it (see Import options).

docs.title: From the Configs page
docs.text: On the Configs page, the tag builder marks a topology with a Builder diagram and opens it in Builder. A topology without a diagram has Import into Builder in its viewer, which opens the Import dialog set to that topology. The tag builder legacy marks a topology from the legacy Builder (see From the Configs page).

docs.title: What an import keeps
docs.text:
• Every node, as a device, with all of its settings, in the order of the config.
  • One network and one switch for each VLAN, with each interface connected to the switch of its VLAN.
